    Chapter 18

    How Cryptography Breaks: Attacks and Pitfalls

    🤔 The math almost never breaks. A missing length check, one duplicated line of code, a signature made of zeros… those do.

    • ⏱️ ~9 min
    • 📚 9 sections
    • 🎮 2 interactive
    • ⭐ 205 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    18.1The math is rarely the weak point#

    Breaking AES-256 or a properly used Ed25519 key by brute force is impossible in practice. So attackers don't try. As cryptographer Adi Shamir put it: "Cryptography is typically bypassed, not penetrated."

    Real attacks go around the math: bad randomness, implementation bugs, misconfigurations, stolen keys, tricked users. There's even a joke term, rubber-hose cryptanalysis: threatening a person until they reveal the key is cheaper than any computation.

    ✔ section read

    18.2A catalog of attacks#

    Attack Plain description Defense
    Brute force Try every possible key Large keys (128+ bits)
    Dictionary / credential stuffing Try common passwords, or passwords leaked from other sites Slow password hashing, MFA, passkeys, rate limits
    Cryptanalysis Find mathematical shortcuts in an algorithm Use well-studied standard algorithms
    Known- / chosen-plaintext Attacker knows or chooses some plaintexts and studies the ciphertexts Modern ciphers are designed to resist this
    Chosen-ciphertext Attacker sends crafted ciphertexts and watches how the system reacts AEAD; uniform error handling
    Man-in-the-middle Intercept and relay, impersonating both sides Authentication: certificates, signatures, fingerprints
    Replay Record a valid message and send it again later Nonces, timestamps, sequence numbers
    Downgrade Trick both sides into using weaker crypto Remove old options; authenticate the negotiation
    Side-channel Learn secrets from timing, power use, electromagnetic radiation, sound or CPU caches Constant-time code, hardware protections
    Fault injection Glitch a chip (voltage, laser, clock) so it makes a revealing mistake Tamper-resistant hardware, result checking
    Padding oracle Use "bad padding" error messages to decrypt data byte by byte AEAD; never reveal why decryption failed
    Nonce / key reuse Reusing a "use-once" value collapses security Counters, random 192-bit nonces, misuse-resistant modes
    Weak randomness Predictable keys OS CSPRNG only
    Implementation bugs Memory errors, skipped checks Well-tested libraries, memory-safe languages, audits, fuzzing
    Key theft Malware, leaked backups, keys committed to Git Hardware key storage, secret scanning, least privilege
    Social engineering Trick a human into giving access Training, phishing-resistant MFA
    Supply chain Compromise a dependency or build system Signed builds, reproducible builds, review
    Quantum (future) Shor's algorithm breaks today's public-key crypto Post-quantum cryptography
    ✔ section read

    18.3Side-channel attacks: secrets leak through the walls#

    Even a mathematically perfect algorithm runs on a physical machine, and machines leak.

    Timing. Imagine a login check that compares a password one character at a time and stops at the first mismatch:

    By measuring tiny time differences, an attacker learns the secret one character at a time: about 26 × 6 = 156 guesses instead of 26⁶ ≈ 300 million. That's why crypto code must run in constant time, taking exactly as long no matter what the secret is (like hmac.compare_digest in Chapter 7).

    Other side channels:

    • Power analysis: a smart card's power use varies with the bits it processes. Recording power traces can reveal its key (demonstrated by Paul Kocher in the late 1990s).
    • Electromagnetic and acoustic: researchers have extracted RSA keys from the faint high-pitched noise a laptop's electronics make (2013).
    • CPU caches and speculative execution: Spectre and Meltdown (2018) showed that one program could read another's secrets through the way modern processors guess ahead.
    ✔ section read

    18.4Replay attacks#

    A replayed message is perfectly genuine. It's just old. If Mallory records "Unlock the car" or "Transfer $100 to Mallory," she can send it again later.

    Defenses: include something that changes every time and is checked by the receiver.

    • Nonces/challenges: the receiver sends a random challenge, and the sender must include it (passkeys work this way).
    • Timestamps: reject messages older than a few seconds or minutes (TOTP, AWS request signing).
    • Sequence numbers: reject repeated or out-of-order numbers (TLS records).
    • Rolling codes: car key fobs send a different code each press.

    18.5Downgrade attacks#

    If two sides negotiate which algorithms to use, an attacker in the middle may try to make them agree on the weakest option.

    📜 FREAK and Logjam (2015). In the 1990s, US export rules required software sold abroad to use deliberately weak "export-grade" crypto, such as 512-bit RSA and Diffie-Hellman keys. Twenty years later, many servers still supported those options. Attackers could trick browsers and servers into using them, then break the weak keys.

    📜 POODLE (2014). Browsers that failed to connect with TLS would "helpfully" retry with SSL 3.0. Attackers could force that failure, then exploit SSL 3.0's padding weakness.

    Defenses: remove old options entirely, and authenticate the negotiation. In TLS 1.3, the Finished messages cover the whole handshake transcript, and the server's random value contains a special marker if it was forced to use an older version.

    ✔ section read

    18.6Padding oracle attacks#

    With CBC mode (Chapter 5), the decrypted data must end with valid padding. If a server responds differently to "bad padding" versus "bad data," an attacker can modify a ciphertext, send it, and watch the reaction. With about 256 tries per byte, they can decrypt the entire message without the key. Serge Vaudenay described this in 2002, and it has broken real systems many times since (including web frameworks and TLS implementations).

    Defense: use AEAD, which checks integrity before decrypting, and fails the same way for every kind of tampering.

    ✔ section read

    18.7Hall of fame (or shame): famous crypto failures#

    1. 2008
      Debian OpenSSL

      What went wrong: A code cleanup removed the randomness source; only 32,768 possible keys

      Lesson: Randomness is everything

    2. 2010
      PlayStation 3

      What went wrong: Same ECDSA nonce for every signature; private key recovered

      Lesson: Never reuse nonces; prefer Ed25519

    3. 2011
      BEAST

      What went wrong: Predictable CBC IVs in TLS 1.0

      Lesson: Upgrade protocols

    4. 2012–13
      CRIME / BREACH

      What went wrong: Compressing data before encryption leaked secrets through the compressed length

      Lesson: Encryption doesn't hide length

    5. 2013
      Lucky Thirteen

      What went wrong: Timing differences in TLS's MAC-then-encrypt CBC mode

      Lesson: Use AEAD

    6. 2014
      Heartbleed

      What went wrong: A missing length check in OpenSSL let anyone read server memory, including private keys. Roughly half a million secure web servers were vulnerable.

      Lesson: Implementation bugs bypass all the math

    7. 2014
      Apple "goto fail"

      What went wrong: One duplicated line of code skipped the certificate signature check

      Lesson: Test the failure paths

    8. 2014
      POODLE

      What went wrong: Downgrade to SSL 3.0 + padding oracle

      Lesson: Remove old protocols

    9. 2015
      FREAK / Logjam

      What went wrong: Leftover 1990s export-grade crypto

      Lesson: Remove weak options completely

    10. 2016
      DROWN

      What went wrong: Servers still supporting SSLv2 exposed TLS sessions that shared the same key

      Lesson: Old protocols endanger new ones

    11. 2016
      Sweet32

      What went wrong: 64-bit block ciphers (3DES, Blowfish) leak data in long sessions

      Lesson: Block size matters

    12. 2017
      ROCA

      What went wrong: A flawed key generator in Infineon security chips produced factorable RSA keys, affecting hundreds of thousands of Estonian national ID cards

      Lesson: Key generation needs scrutiny too

    13. 2017
      KRACK

      What went wrong: WPA2 handshake replays caused nonce reuse

      Lesson: Protocol state machines are tricky

    14. 2017
      ROBOT

      What went wrong: Bleichenbacher's 1998 RSA padding attack still worked on major sites

      Lesson: Old attacks return; drop RSA key transport

    15. 2020
      CurveBall

      What went wrong: Windows didn't fully check elliptic-curve parameters in certificates, allowing spoofed certificates (reported by the NSA)

      Lesson: Validate every field

    16. 2022
      "Psychic signatures"

      What went wrong: Java accepted an ECDSA signature made of all zeros as valid for anything

      Lesson: Check the obvious edge cases

    17. 2023
      Terrapin

      What went wrong: An attacker could silently drop messages at the start of some SSH connections

      Lesson: Authenticate the whole handshake

    18. 2024
      xz backdoor

      What went wrong: A malicious contributor hid a backdoor targeting SSH inside a compression library

      Lesson: Supply chain and trust in people

    18.8Don't roll your own crypto#

    The first rule of practical cryptography: don't invent your own algorithms or protocols, and don't implement standard ones yourself for real use.

    The idea is often called Schneier's Law (after security expert Bruce Schneier): anyone can design a cipher that they personally can't break. That proves nothing. Only years of attack by many experts build confidence. Even world-class experts produce designs that are later broken, which is why standards go through long public competitions.

    Instead, use well-reviewed libraries, preferably their high-level interfaces that make safe choices for you:

    Need Use
    General-purpose crypto with safe defaults libsodium (C; bindings like PyNaCl for Python), Google Tink (Java, C++, Go, Python)
    Python cryptography (prefer its high-level recipes like Fernet; the "hazmat" layer is for experts)
    Go The standard library's crypto/... packages
    Browsers / JavaScript The Web Crypto API (crypto.subtle)
    TLS Your platform's TLS (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC, rustls, Go's crypto/tls, the OS's built-in TLS)
    Encrypting files age, GnuPG
    Password hashing Argon2id via a maintained library (e.g. argon2-cffi), or your web framework's built-in password hasher

    For example, Fernet in Python does authenticated symmetric encryption (AES plus HMAC, with a timestamp) with no decisions to get wrong:

    Python
    from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

key = Fernet.generate_key()       # store this safely (see Chapter 19)
f = Fernet(key)
token = f.encrypt(b"my secret note")
print(f.decrypt(token))           # b'my secret note'
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Rolling your own crypto

    ❌ Avoid
    Home-made crypto

    “I invented a cipher!”

    • A great way to learn (in a sandbox)
    • Unreviewed; side channels; misuse
    • Experts get it wrong too
    Best for: Learning projects only
    ✅ Use it
    Vetted libraries

    libsodium, Tink, platform crypto

    • Reviewed, tested, constant time
    • Safe high-level APIs
    • Must still be used correctly and kept updated
    Best for: Every production system

    18.9Developer mistakes checklist#

    ❌ Mistake ✅ Do this instead
    Using ECB mode AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305
    Encryption without integrity (plain CBC or CTR) AEAD
    Reusing nonces or IVs Counters, or random nonces with XChaCha20; or a library that handles it
    Hard-coding keys or committing them to Git A secrets manager or KMS; secret scanning (Chapter 19)
    MD5, SHA-1 or plain SHA-256 for passwords Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt
    random, Math.random() for tokens or keys secrets, crypto.getRandomValues(), OS CSPRNG
    Turning off certificate verification Fix the certificate or trust store properly
    Comparing MACs/tokens with == Constant-time comparison
    Using a raw Diffie-Hellman output as a key Run it through HKDF
    Textbook RSA or PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption RSA-OAEP, or better, HPKE / X25519-based encryption
    Trusting the JWT alg header Enforce the expected algorithm server-side
    Logging secrets, tokens or full card numbers Redact sensitive fields in logs
    Supporting TLS 1.0/1.1, SSLv3, RC4, 3DES TLS 1.2+ with AEAD; TLS 1.3 preferred
    Treating Base64 or hex as "encryption" Actual encryption
    Never rotating keys; no plan for compromise Rotation schedules and a tested revocation procedure
    Designing your own protocol TLS, Noise, Signal Protocol, HPKE, age
